doc.title: Ray Ricker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 27, 2022

title: Arriving at Eastman: Rayburn Wright, Chuck Mangione and touring
summary: In 1970 Ricker became Rayburn Wright's assistant, saw Mangione's rising fame, and joined his tours and recordings including Red Rocks.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you about Chuck Mangione. So I’m moving ahead a little bit and you’re at Eastman and Chuck was well known locally. Was he doing like an adjunct at Eastman at that time?

Yeah he was. When I went Rayburn Wright was also the first year that Ray Wright came, he came from Radio City Music Hall where he was the music director of that. He worked his way up through the arranging ranks and ended up as the head musical guy at Radio City. And he had been teaching some courses in the summer at Eastman, some arranging courses, called “The Arranger’s Workshop.” And he was then, thought it was time for him to move from the city and have a little less hectic life — not less busy though because you know you don’t go to these jobs to try to retire because you’re building things and you know working hard. But anyway he came to Eastman in 1970 and that was the first year that I was there. And I was assigned as his graduate assistant and so that turned out to be a very good thing. Now Chuck had been directing the jazz ensemble for the previous couple of years. He continued conducting the jazz ensemble during that time when Ray came, and Ray did all the arranging and those kinds of things and formed a studio orchestra which was the jazz ensemble with strings. And yeah, so Chuck was a formidable guy there. He was gaining recognition. By this time he had his first I don’t know if it was his first one but the first one that kind of hit, that was a big production with strings and everything — I mean the concert was called “Friends and Love.” So all that popularity poured over to us in school. And we were, you know we’d do jazz © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

ensemble concerts and there’d be 3,000 people there. The Eastman Theater would be packed. And they weren’t charging anything. Still, to get 3,000 people for a school show, you know, was pretty impressive. And so that happened and Chuck continued to gain popularity and because of that he started doing bigger records and doing some tours and I was lucky to play in his expanded group that did tours. We did tours of the East Coast and Midwest. He had me come to California once to do a recording there in Herb Alpert’s, what is that A&R —

Yeah. So, yeah and I got to go back home and play in Red Rocks once. So Chuck, he liked me and he liked the things I could do. And because he liked friendly faces in the group you know, and if it was possible he would help people out. There were some other people I mean Jeff Tyzik played a lot of these tours too, and helped on a lot of the recordings.
